description: In io_uring's io-wq worker pool, cancelling a hashed bucket-0 work item whose list predecessor is non-hashed causes io_wq_remove_pending() to install the non-hashed io_kiocb as wq->hash_tail[0], since io_get_work_hash() returns 0 for all non-hashed work. The non-hashed request completes and is freed via req_cachep while hash_tail[0] still points at it, and because hash_tail[] lives on the per-task io_wq it survives ring close. The next hashed bucket-0 enqueue writes an 8-byte kernel heap pointer to offset 216 of the freed 256-byte slab slot via wq_list_add_after(). An unprivileged local attacker controls the SQE sequence needed to trigger this deterministically, and by cross-cache reclaiming the freed page with pipe_buffer arrays can land the write on pipe_buffer.flags, set PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE on a spliced page-cache page, and perform a Dirty Pipe overwrite of a SUID binary to gain root. Demonstrated on Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04, Debian 11/13, Fedora 41, Rocky 9 (io_uring re-enabled), Alpine 3.21, and mainline HEAD.
reproduction: 1. Pin task and limit io-wq to one bound worker; find a tmpfs file that hashes to bucket 0.
2. Submit a 4-SQE batch: B=FSYNC on a dirtied ext4 file (blocks the worker), N=FSYNC (non-hashed), H=WRITEV on the bucket-0 file (hashed), C=ASYNC_CANCEL(H).
3. CANCEL runs inline while the pending list is [N, H]; io_wq_remove_pending(H, prev=N) plants wq->hash_tail[0] = &N->work.

4. Let N complete, flush the per-ring io_kiocb cache (drain-NOP on 6.16+, or munmap+close the ring and wait for io_ring_exit_work on older kernels), and wait out the RCU grace period so N is freed to SLUB.

5. Free N's slab neighbours so the page returns to the buddy allocator, then spray thousands of pipes with F_SETPIPE_SZ to reclaim the page as kmalloc-cg-64 pipe_buffer[1] arrays; offset 256*K+216 lands on pipe_buffer.flags for every K.
6. splice() one byte of the SUID binary's entry-point page into every sprayed pipe.
7. Submit another hashed bucket-0 WRITEV; io_wq_insert_work() writes &new_io_kiocb->work.list (low byte 0xD8, bit 4 set) into the victim pipe_buffer.flags, setting PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE.
8. write() shellcode to every pipe; the corrupted one merges into the SUID binary's page-cache page.
9. execve() the SUID binary; shellcode runs as root. Retry on miss (~10-25% per attempt).
technical_details:
Hi --

I believe I've found another local privilege escalation vulnerability

in the kernel. This one is in io_uring's io-wq worker pool and doesn't

require a second leak: it's a pure data-corruption chain that ends at

Dirty Pipe. The vuln itself is five years old and affects every kernel

since 5.7. I've gotten root with it on Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/ 26.04,

Debian 11/13, Fedora 41, Rocky 9, Alpine 3.21, and mainline HEAD.

(As in my prior bugs, I used an LLM to find this, and to write and

port the exploit.)

The vulnerability is in io_wq_remove_pending(), in io_uring/io-wq.c.

io-wq is io_uring's worker thread pool, used to run requests that

can't complete inline. Each task has one io-wq (tctx->io_wq). Pending

work is kept on a singly-linked list (acct->work_list). Write-type ops

on regular files (WRITEV, WRITE, FALLOCATE, etc.) are "hashed" by file

inode so writes to the same file run serially rather than in parallel,

and the tail of each inode's chain is cached in wq->hash_tail[bucket]

so new work can be appended after it. Reads, NOPs, FSYNC, and

everything else are "non-hashed" and any free worker can run them

concurrently.

IORING_OP_ASYNC_CANCEL lets a user remove a pending work item before a

worker dequeues it, which goes through io_wq_remove_pending(). If the

cancelled item was the tail of its hash bucket, this function has to

decide what the new tail should be. It does that by comparing the

predecessor's hash value:

    static inline void io_wq_remove_pending(struct io_wq *wq,

                                            struct io_wq_acct *acct,

                                            struct io_wq_work *work,

                                            struct io_wq_work_node *prev)

    {

        unsigned int hash = io_get_work_hash(work);

        struct io_wq_work *prev_work = NULL;

        if (io_wq_is_hashed(work) && work == wq->hash_tail[hash]) {

            if (prev)

                prev_work = container_of(prev, struct io_wq_work, list);

            if (prev_work && io_get_work_hash(prev_work) == hash)

                wq->hash_tail[hash] = prev_work;

            else

                wq->hash_tail[hash] = NULL;

        }

        wq_list_del(&acct->work_list, &work->list, prev);

    }

The outer condition correctly checks that the cancelled work is

hashed. But the inner one does not check that the *predecessor* is.

This matters because io_get_work_hash() is not a reliable

discriminator: it's just `atomic_read(&work->flags) >> 24`, and the

hash bits are never set on non-hashed work, so it returns 0 for every

non-hashed work item---which is also a valid bucket number. So when a

hashed bucket-0 work (about 1/64 of regular files) is cancelled while

a non-hashed work happens to be its list predecessor, the check `0 ==

0` spuriously passes and a pointer to the non-hashed io_kiocb is

stored in wq->hash_tail[0]. This work item that is never part of any

hash chain and never will be.

Because non-hashed work is dequeued via the fast path in

io_get_next_work(), which never touches hash_tail[], nothing ever

clears that stale pointer. The non-hashed io_kiocb completes normally,

goes back to the per-ring request cache, and is eventually

kmem_cache_free()'d to req_cachep---at which point wq->hash_tail[0] is

a dangling pointer into freed slab. And the io_wq that holds

hash_tail[] is per-*task* (tctx->io_wq), not per-ring. Closing the

ring only sets a worker-exit flag and never touches hash_tail[]. The

dangling pointer therefore persists for the lifetime of the task,

across ring open/close.

The next hashed bucket-0 enqueue on that io_wq dereferences the

dangling pointer in io_wq_insert_work() executes this code:

    tail = wq->hash_tail[hash];     /* dangling */

    wq->hash_tail[hash] = work;

    if (!tail)

        goto append;                /* not taken */

    wq_list_add_after(&work->list, &tail->list, &acct->work_list);

wq_list_add_after() does `pos->next = node` into the freed object at

offsetof(io_kiocb, work.list.next) == 216. This gives the attack

primitive, an 8-byte write of a kernel heap pointer

(&new_io_kiocb->work.list) into offset 216 of a freed 256-byte

io_kiocb slab slot.

I think this was introduced by 204361a77f40 ("io-wq: fix hang after

cancelling pending hashed work", 2020-08-23), which added this

predecessor fixup and was Cc: stable@ # 5.7+.

The attached crasher.c is a minimal KASAN trigger. It pins the task

and the io-wq worker to CPU 0 and limits the io-wq to a single bound

worker. Then it iterates over tmpfs files (~1/64 of which land in

bucket 0), and per file submits a four-SQE batch in one

io_uring_enter(). I'll call the four requests B (a blocker), N (the

non-hashed predecessor that gets planted in hash_tail), H (the

hashed work that gets cancelled), and C (the cancel):

    B: FSYNC(ext4_blocker)    bound, non-hashed, keeps the worker busy

    N: FSYNC(f)               bound, non-hashed

    H: WRITEV(f)              bound, hashed  (WRITEV has hash_reg_file)

    C: ASYNC_CANCEL(H)        inline

The blocker is a freshly-dirtied ext4 file, so the single worker

sits in vfs_fsync() for milliseconds; by the time the inline CANCEL

runs, the pending list is [N, H]. io_wq_remove_pending(H, prev=&N)

fires with N as the non-hashed predecessor and plants hash_tail[0]

= &N->work. After N completes, a NOP with IOSQE_IO_DRAIN flushes

the per-ring cache (io_drain_req -> io_queue_deferred ->

__io_req_caches_free -> kmem_cache_free(req_cachep, N)), a

membarrier(GLOBAL) waits out the SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU grace period,

and a second WRITEV on the same file dereferences the dangling

hash_tail[0]. Under a KASAN kernel this reports slab-use-after-free

in io_wq_enqueue within a few seconds, running as a plain

unprivileged user.

One detail that cost me (rather: my LLM) some time is that none of

these SQEs can use IOSQE_ASYNC. With IOSQE_ASYNC, io_submit_sqe()

routes the request to io_queue_sqe_fallback() -> io_queue_iowq() ->

io_prep_async_work() *before* io_assign_file() runs, so req->file is

NULL and the REQ_F_ISREG hashing branch is skipped. Without it, FSYNC

and tmpfs-WRITEV both take -EAGAIN from io_issue_sqe() (which has

assigned req->file) and punt through io_queue_async() ->

io_queue_iowq() with req->file set, which is the path that hashes.

The drain-NOP cache flush the crasher uses was added in commit

8fb7aee05591 and first appears in v6.16, so the crasher as attached

targets HEAD and other 6.16+ kernels; older kernels need to close the

ring and wait for io_ring_exit_work() instead (see below).

The attached exploit.c turns this UAF write into an LPE.

To recap what we have: after the trigger, hash_tail[0] points at a

freed io_kiocb (call it N) somewhere on a slab page owned by

req_cachep. The next hashed bucket-0 enqueue will write an 8-byte

kernel heap pointer to N + 216. I don't get to choose the value

written---it's whatever address the new io_kiocb happens to be

allocated at---and I don't get to choose when the slot gets reused.

So this is a narrow primitive: one write of an uncontrolled value to

a fixed offset inside freed memory.

The exploit's job is to put something at N + 216 where writing an

uncontrolled kernel pointer does something useful. The exploit targets

struct pipe_buffer.flags, because it has two properties that make it

tolerate an uncontrolled write:

  - Only one bit of .flags matters: anon_pipe_write() tests

    PIPE_BUF_FLAG_CAN_MERGE (bit 4, 0x10). A pipe is a ring of

    pipe_buffers, each one holding a reference to a page and a .flags

    field. Anonymous pipe data carries CAN_MERGE so small write()s can

    append into the existing page instead of allocating a new one. But

    a pipe_buffer that was filled by splice()ing file content in

    references the file's *page-cache* page directly, and splice

    deliberately leaves CAN_MERGE clear --- merging into that page

    would silently modify the cached file. If an attacker can set

    CAN_MERGE on a spliced buffer, a plain write() to the pipe

    scribbles into the page cache of a read-only file. That's the

    Dirty Pipe bug (CVE-2022-0847). I'm re-creating the bad state

    through the UAF rather than the original pipe_init() bug.

  - The uncontrolled write happens to set that bit. The value

    written is &H2->work.list where H2 is a live io_kiocb. io_kiocb

    is 248 bytes, HWCACHE-aligned to a 256-byte slot, and work is at

    offset 216 --- so the written pointer is always

    (some multiple of 256) + 216, and its low byte is always

    216 == 0xD8. 0xD8 has bit 4 set, so CAN_MERGE is set. The other

    bits in 0xD8 and the garbage in the upper bytes of .flags aren't

    consulted by pipe_write().

So the plan is to arrange for N + 216 to be the .flags field of a live

pipe_buffer that's holding a page-cache page of a SUID binary, then

trigger the write, then Dirty Pipe. Two things stand in the way:

  - req_cachep is a dedicated slab cache that only holds io_kiocb,

    so I can't reclaim N's slot directly with a pipe_buffer. But all

    slab caches draw their backing pages from the same page

    allocator (the "buddy" allocator), so I can reclaim at the page

    level instead: free every io_kiocb on N's slab page, SLUB

    returns the empty page to the buddy allocator, and a

    kmalloc-cg-64 allocation pulls the same page back as its own

    fresh slab. pipe2() followed by fcntl(F_SETPIPE_SZ, 4096)

    allocates a pipe_buffer[1] array via kcalloc(1, 40), which goes

    to kmalloc-cg-64, so spraying a few thousand pipes reclaims the

    page with pipe_buffer arrays. This is the fragile part of the

    exploit; see the per-kernel notes below.

  - I don't know where N was on its page. io_kiocb slots are at

    bytes 0, 256, 512, ..., 3840 of the page --- 256*K for K in

    0..15, 16 slots, and SLUB chose K. After the cross-cache the

    same page holds 64-byte kmalloc-cg-64 slots, and I need

    256*K + 216 to land on a pipe_buffer's .flags for *any* K.

    Conveniently it does:

        256*K + 216 = 64*(4K + 3) + 24

    i.e. slot (4K + 3) at byte 24, for every K in 0..15. And

    offsetof(struct pipe_buffer, flags) == 24. So I don't need to

    know K.

Putting it together, the attack tries to trigger the plant; free N and

its slab-mates and wait for the page to reach the buddy allocator;

spray pipes sized to one pipe_buffer; splice() one byte of a SUID

binary's entry-point page into every pipe; trigger the write; write()

shellcode to every pipe (the one with the stomped .flags merges it

into the SUID binary's page cache); execve() the SUID binary. When it

works, the shellcode runs as root. The cross-cache reclaim is

probabilistic, so the exploit retries if it fails. My observed success

rate is roughly 10-25% per attempt, and it typically lands within

10-150 attempts, under a minute or two.

I've verified that this exploit affects a number of distro kernels. At

the bottom of the email I've provided some analysis of what's

necessary to tweak for each of the attacks. (The per-kernel tweaks are

all in the grooming and cross-cache stages; the bug, the UAF write,

and the Dirty Pipe payload are identical everywhere.)

I've also attached a patch that adds the missing io_wq_is_hashed()

check on the predecessor. This is the smallest change I could find

that fixes the vulnerability, but I don't know if it's the right

change (maybe hash_tail should just always be cleared on cancel and

re-established on the next enqueue?). Feel free to disregard.

Thanks,

Nicholas

Attached:

  - crasher.c: minimal KASAN reproducer, runs as any unprivileged

    user. Needs a tmpfs /tmp and an ext4 /var/tmp (or cwd); does

    not need a SUID target. Targets HEAD / 6.16+ (uses the

    drain-NOP cache flush).

  - exploit.c: the LPE for HEAD / Ubuntu 26.04 / Ubuntu 24.04 HWE

    (kernels where offsetof(io_kiocb, work) = 216, the dedicated

    req_cachep cache exists, and the drain-NOP cache flush is

    present). Targets a SUID ELF at /suid_target whose _start is at

    file offset 0x80 (see reproduction notes). Ports to other

    kernels per the list above with changes to the pipe_buffer

    retarget, the cache-flush mechanism, and the grooming

    constants.

  - root_helper.c: a tiny root-owned helper the shellcode execves.

  - 0001-io-wq-check-that-the-predecessor-is-hashed-in-io_wq_.patch

      --- a/io_uring/io-wq.c

      +++ b/io_uring/io-wq.c

      @@ io_wq_remove_pending @@

           if (io_wq_is_hashed(work) && work == wq->hash_tail[hash]) {

               if (prev)

                   prev_work = container_of(prev, struct io_wq_work, list);

      -        if (prev_work && io_get_work_hash(prev_work) == hash)

      +        if (prev_work && io_wq_is_hashed(prev_work) &&

      +            io_get_work_hash(prev_work) == hash)

                   wq->hash_tail[hash] = prev_work;

               else

                   wq->hash_tail[hash] = NULL;

           }

Reproduction of the LPE on stock Ubuntu 26.04 (the attached

exploit.c runs here unmodified):

  wget

https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/daily/server/resolute/current/resolute-server-cloudimg-amd64.img

  cat > user-data <<'EOF'

  #cloud-config

  password: test

  chpasswd: { expire: False }

  ssh_pwauth: True

  EOF

  printf 'instance-id: x\nlocal-hostname: x\n' > meta-data

  genisoimage -output seed.iso -volid cidata -joliet -rock user-data

meta-data

  qemu-img create -f qcow2 -F qcow2 \

    -b resolute-server-cloudimg-amd64.img disk.qcow2 8G

  qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -m 2G -smp 2 -nographic \

    -drive file=disk.qcow2,if=virtio \

    -drive file=seed.iso,if=virtio,format=raw \

    -netdev user,id=n0,hostfwd=tcp::2222-:22 -device virtio-net,netdev=n0

  # compile statically on the host (cloud image has no gcc):

  gcc -O2 -static -o exploit exploit.c

  gcc -O2 -static -o root_helper root_helper.c

  scp -P 2222 exploit root_helper ubuntu@localhost:/tmp/   # password 'test'

  # ssh -p 2222 ubuntu@localhost, then set up the SUID test target

  # (this is test scaffolding only -- any SUID ELF with a few bytes

  #  of writable entry-point padding works; the exploit hijacks it

  #  via page-cache write, the file on disk is never touched):

  sudo install -o root -m 0755 /tmp/root_helper /root_helper

  python3 - <<'PY' | sudo tee /suid_target >/dev/null

  import struct,sys

  # minimal static x86-64 ELF, _start at file offset 0x80 = 128 NOPs +

exit(0)

  eh = struct.pack('<4s5B7x2HI3QI6H', b'\x7fELF',2,1,1,0,0, 2,0x3e, 1,

       0x400080, 0x40, 0, 0, 64, 56, 1, 0, 0, 0)

  ph = struct.pack('<2I6Q', 1,5, 0, 0x400000, 0x400000, 0x200, 0x200,

0x1000)

  body = b'\x90'*128 + b'\x48\x31\xff\x6a\x3c\x58\x0f\x05'

sys.stdout.buffer.write(((eh+ph).ljust(0x80,b'\0')+body).ljust(0x200,b'\0'))

  PY

  sudo chmod 4755 /suid_target

  sudo useradd -m testuser

  sudo install -o testuser /tmp/exploit /home/testuser/exploit

  sudo -u testuser -i

  id

  # uid=1001(testuser) gid=1001(testuser)

  ./exploit

  # [*] io_uring io-wq hash_tail[] UAF -> Dirty Pipe LPE

  # [*] uid=1001 euid=1001

  # [*] probing 384 ramfs files for io-wq hash bucket 0...

  # [+] f7 hashes to bucket 0 (candidate 1/4)

  # ...

  # [*] attempt  4/80: W merged=1

  # [+] Dirty Pipe write landed -- /suid_target hijacked

  # [*] execve(/suid_target)

  # uid=0 gid=0 euid=0 egid=0

  # root@...# id; head -1 /etc/shadow

  # uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),1001(testuser)

  # root:$y$j9T$...:20584:0:99999:7:::

For the KASAN crasher, build HEAD with KASAN:

  git clone

https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/torvalds/linux.git

  cd linux

  make defconfig

  scripts/config -e KASAN -e KASAN_GENERIC

  make olddefconfig

  make -j$(nproc) bzImage

boot with any rootfs, and run ./crasher unprivileged; expect a

slab-use-after-free in io_wq_enqueue within a few seconds.

Impact:

  * Linux HEAD (7.1.0-rc2-g81d6f7807536, x86_64_defconfig) -- the

    reference target. offsetof(io_kiocb, work) = 216, kmalloc-cg-64.

    Root.

  * Ubuntu 26.04 (7.0.0-14-generic) -- the attached exploit.c ran

    unchanged from the HEAD build. All offsets identical. Root on

    attempt 4 and 9 of 80, under 10 seconds each.

  * Ubuntu 24.04 HWE (6.17.0-23-generic) -- ran unchanged. Same

    offsets, and 6.17 has the drain-NOP cache flush. 6.17 is still

    classic SLUB (the per-CPU sheaf allocator the HEAD exploit was

    tuned against landed in 7.0) but the grooming constants worked

    anyway. Root on attempt 5 and 13.

  * Debian 13 / trixie (6.12.86+deb13-amd64) -- same offsets.

    Pre-v6.16 kernels don't flush the per-ring io_kiocb free list

    from io_queue_deferred(), so the exploit has to munmap() and

    close() the trigger ring and wait for io_ring_exit_work() to

    free the cache (munmap is needed because the SQ/CQ/SQE mappings

    hold vm_file references; close() alone doesn't start teardown).

    io_ring_exit_work runs on an unbound kworker on a different

    CPU, so N's freed page lands deep in that CPU's PCP free list;

    the pipe spray was raised to 8000 and split across both CPUs.

    Root 3/3 cold runs.

  * Alpine 3.21 (linux-virt 6.12.81-0) -- same offsets, same

    pre-v6.16 close-and-reopen workaround as Debian 13. One

    Alpine-specific trap: the default pipe is 8 slots (a 320-byte

    pipe_buffer array on an order-1 slab page), so shrinking

    straight to 1 slot frees enough order-1 pages to trip the

    buddy allocator's free_high heuristic and drain the whole PCP

    mid-spray, evicting N's page before it can be reclaimed. The

    port shrinks the pipes in a step that keeps the frees order-0.

    Root, ~1 in 2-5 cold boots.

  * Fedora 41 (6.11.4-301.fc41) -- same offsets. Same pre-v6.16

    close-and-reopen ring workaround, and the pipe spray runs from

    both CPUs to chase the unbound kworker. SELinux enforcing

    (targeted policy) doesn't help---the exploit's syscall surface

    is all allowed for unconfined_t. Root on attempt 15 and 18.

  * Rocky Linux 9.7 / RHEL 9 (5.14.0-611.5.1.el9_7) -- same

    offsets (216). Same two-ring close-and-reopen, and the spray

    alternates CPUs. The important caveat: RHEL 9 ships

    kernel.io_uring_disabled=2 by default, which hard-disables

    io_uring for everyone and blocks the bug completely. I had to

    set it to 0 to test. Any system that's re-enabled io_uring

    (Podman, PostgreSQL 17+, QEMU) is fully exploitable. Root on

    attempt 17/200 under Enforcing.

  * Ubuntu 24.04 GA and 22.04 HWE (both 6.8.0-xx-generic) --

    offsetof(io_kiocb, work) is 208 on 6.8, not 216.

    256*K + 208 lands on pipe_buffer.ops in kmalloc-cg-64, which

    is a guaranteed oops. I retargeted kmalloc-cg-192

    (F_SETPIPE_SZ(16384) -> kcalloc(4, 40) -> pipe_buffer[4]);

    the write then lands on pipe_buffer[3].flags for 5 of 16

    slots. The low byte is 0xD0 instead of 0xD8, but

    0xD0 & CAN_MERGE is still set. Also needed the two-ring

    close workaround and munmap() of the SQ/CQ/SQE mappings

    (close() alone doesn't drop the last vm_file reference on

    6.8). Root on attempt 1-16 across runs.

  * Ubuntu 22.04 GA (5.15.0-173-generic) -- offsetof(io_kiocb,

    work) is 184 on 5.15, and io_kiocb is merged into the shared

    :A-0000256 cache rather than a dedicated cache. Retargeted

    kmalloc-cg-96 (F_SETPIPE_SZ(8192) -> pipe_buffer[2]); 5/16

    slots land on .flags, low byte 0xB8 (CAN_MERGE still set).

    5.15's classic SLUB plus LIFO free order means N's slab page

    parks on the per-CPU partial list and never reaches buddy; a

    post-trigger POLL_ADD burst pushes enough extra pages through

    to discard it. Root on attempt 17/120.

  * Debian 11 / bullseye (5.10.0-42-amd64, 5.10.251-4) -- the

    oldest kernel I tried. offsetof(io_kiocb, work) is 184;

    merged :A-0000256 cache (and no kmalloc-cg-* split yet on

    5.10). Retargeted kmalloc-96 / pipe_buffer[2]; same 5/16

    alignment as 5.15, low byte 0xB8. The per-ring recycle cache

    on 5.10 is very aggressive and NOPs never hit SLUB, so the

    groom uses POLL_ADDs on a never-readable pipe (each one holds

    its io_kiocb until ring teardown). Plus a pre-drain of 768

    pipes to exhaust the shared cache's partial slabs. Root on

    attempt 10/150.

  * Debian 12 / bookworm (6.1.0-47-amd64, 6.1.170-3) -- the bug

    is present and I demonstrated the UAF write, a kernel-heap

    pointer infoleak (via a reclaimed signalfd's /proc fdinfo),

    and a kernel panic on close. But offsetof(io_kiocb, work) is

    200 on 6.1, and 256*K + 200 mod 64 == 8 lands on

    pipe_buffer.offset, not .flags. I didn't find a reclaim

    target that lines up on 6.1; the Dirty Pipe chain as written

    didn't port. The memory-safety violation, infoleak, and DoS

    are all demonstrated regardless.
title: LPE via io_uring io-wq worker pool
